# Overall objectives

- understand computational challenges related to large array data and key strategies to address them
- gain hands-on Python experience and increase confidence in handling large array data
- appreciate the diversity of the open-source Python ecosystem for large array data and how you are part of it

## Schedule

- day 1: basics, motivation, reading and writing large arrays
- day 2: processing large arrays in parallel, standards for large imaging data
- day 3: advanced topics and case studies: compression, benchmarking, visualisation, real-life applications
- day 4-5: collaboration

## What is an array?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
* Data arranged in an (N-dimensional) grid
* Data all have the same type
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
![](img/array_2d.png){.nostretch width="90%"}
:::
:::

## What is an array?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
Arrays have type and shape.
:::

::: {.column width="59%"}
```{.python}
import numpy as np

array_shape = (5,6)
dtype = np.uint8
array = np.random.randint(low=0, high=2**8, size=array_shape, dtype=dtype)

print(array)
print("Array shape: "+str(array.shape))
array_bytes = array.tobytes()
```
:::
:::

:::footer
[@stansby_introduction_2026]
:::

## Data size

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
Arrays have type and shape.
:::

::: {.column width="59%"}
```{python}
import numpy as np

array_shape = (5,6)
dtype = np.uint8
np.random.seed = 42
array = np.random.randint(
    low=0, high=2**8, 
    size=array_shape, 
    dtype=dtype
)

print(array)
print("Array shape: "+str(array.shape))
```
:::
:::

:::footer
[@stansby_introduction_2026]
:::

## Array size

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
Computers store data as _bits_ , arranged in _bytes_ of 8 bits.
We use the usual decimal system prefixes:

* kilobyte (KB)
* megabyte (MB)
* gigabyte (GB)
* terabyte (TB)

:::

::: {.column width="59%"}
```{.python}

...

array_bytes = arr.tobytes()
print(f"{len(array_bytes)} bytes total")
print()
print("First ten bytes:")
for my_byte in array_bytes[:10]:
    print(f'{my_byte:0>8b}', end=' ')

print("...")
```
:::
:::

## Array size

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
Computers store data as _bits_, arranged in _bytes_ of 8 bits.
We use the usual decimal system prefixes:

* kilobyte (KB)
* megabyte (MB)
* gigabyte (GB)
* terabyte (TB)

:::

::: {.column width="59%"}
```{python}
import numpy as np

array_shape = (5,5)
dtype = np.uint8
np.random.seed = 42
array = np.random.randint(low=0, high=2**8, size=array_shape, dtype=dtype)
array_bytes = array.tobytes()

print(f"{len(array_bytes)} bytes total")
print()
print("First ten bytes:")
for my_byte in array_bytes[:10]:
    print(f'{my_byte:0>8b}', end=' ')

print("...")
```
:::
:::

:::footer
[@stansby_introduction_2026]
:::

## Array size

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
Computers store data as _bits_ , arranged in _bytes_ of 8 bits.
There are also binary system equivalents

* kibibyte (KiB) = 1024 bytes
* mebibyte (MiB) = 1024 kibibytes
* ...

We treat KB and KiB as equivalent for our purposes.

## Geography

<div id="map" style="height: 550px;"></div>

<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://unpkg.com/leaflet@1.9.4/dist/leaflet.css"/>
<script src="https://unpkg.com/leaflet@1.9.4/dist/leaflet.js"></script>

<script>
let map;
function initMap() {
  if (map) return;
  map = L.map('map', {
    center: [51.5204, -0.1385],
    zoom: 16,
    preferCanvas: true
  });
  L.tileLayer('https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png', {
    maxZoom: 19,
    attribution: '&copy; OpenStreetMap contributors'
  }).addTo(map);

  L.marker([51.5204, -0.1385])
    .addTo(map)
    .bindPopup('25 Howland St')
    .openPopup();
}

Reveal.on('slidechanged', event => {
  if (event.currentSlide.querySelector('#map')) {
    initMap();
    setTimeout(() => map.invalidateSize(), 200);
  }
});
</script>

Computers store data as _bits_ , arranged in _bytes_ of 8 bits
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{.python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

array_shape = (32, 32)
dtype = np.uint16
image = np.random.randint(low=0, high=2**16, size=array_shape, dtype=dtype)
print(image)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.imshow(image, cmap="Grays", vmin=0, vmax=2**16);
```

Using `numpy` keeps your code simple, more accessible, and easy-to-read.
